'''Christine Darden''' ([[née]] '''Mann'''; born September 10, 1942) is an American [[aeronautical engineer]] who devoted much of her 40-year career in aerodynamics at [[NASA]] to research  [[supersonic flight]] and [[sonic boom]]s. She was the first African-American woman at [[NASA]]'s [[Langley Research Center]] to be promoted to the [[Senior Executive Service (United States)|Senior Executive Service]], the top rank in the federal civil service.

Darden is one of the researchers featured in the book ''[[Hidden Figures (book)|Hidden Figures]]: The American Dream and the Untold Story of the Black Women Mathematicians Who Helped Win the Space Race'' (2016), a history of some of the influential African-American women mathematicians and engineers at NASA in the mid-20th century, by [[Margot Lee Shetterly]].<ref name=hidden/>

In 2019, Darden was awarded the [[Congressional Gold Medal]].<ref name="congress">{{cite web |title=H.R.1396 - Hidden Figures Congressional Gold Medal Act |url=https://www.congress.gov/bill/116th-congress/house-bill/1396?q=%7B%22search%22%3A%5B%22hr1396%22%5D%7D&r=1&s=1 |website=Congress.gov | date=8 November 2019 |access-date=9 November 2019}}</ref>

==Early life and education==

Christine Mann was born September 10, 1942, to schoolteacher Desma l. Cheney and insurance agent Noah Horace Mann Sr. in [[Monroe, North Carolina]]. Both parents encouraged her to pursue a quality education.<ref name=":0" /> Starting from age three, Darden was brought by her mother to her own classroom where she taught, and at age four, Darden was enrolled in kindergarten. During elementary school, Darden took a great interest in breaking apart and reconstructing mechanical objects like her bicycle.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book|title=Distinguished African American Scientists of the 20th Century|last1=Kessler|first1=James H.|last2=Kidd|first2=J.S. |last3=Kidd|first3=Renée S.|last4=Morin|first4=Katherine A.|publisher=[[Greenwood Publishing Group]] |year=1996|isbn=9780897749558 |location=Phoenix, Arizona|pages=[https://archive.org/details/distinguishedafr00kess/page/60 60–63]|url=https://archive.org/details/distinguishedafr00kess/page/60}}</ref> Darden finished her last two years of primary school at [[Allen School (Asheville, North Carolina)|Allen High School]], a boarding school in [[Asheville, North Carolina]].

She graduated as the class [[valedictorian]] in 1958, subsequently receiving a scholarship to attend [[Hampton University]], a [[historically black college]] then known as Hampton Institute. During her studies at Hampton, she participated in some of the early protests of the [[Civil Rights Movement]].<ref name=hidden>{{Cite book|title=Hidden Figures: The American Dream and the Untold Story of the Black Women Mathematicians Who Helped Win the Space Race|last=Shetterly|first=Margot Lee|publisher=[[HarperCollins]] |year=2016|isbn=9780062363596|location=New York, United States|pages=[https://archive.org/details/hiddenfiguresame0000shet/page/202 202]|url=https://archive.org/details/hiddenfiguresame0000shet/page/202}}</ref> She participated in several student [[sit-in]]s alongside her other Black peers.<ref name=":2" /> Mann graduated from Hampton with a B.S. in Mathematics in 1962. She also earned a teaching certification, and taught high school mathematics for a brief time.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=http://www.nasa.gov/centers/langley/news/researchernews/rn_CDarden.html |title=NASA - Standing on the Shoulders of a Computer|website=www.nasa.gov|date=29 March 2013 |language=en|access-date=2016-09-09}}</ref>

== Career ==

=== Teaching ===
In 1963, Mann married Walter L. Darden Jr., a middle-school science teacher. In 1965 she became a research assistant at [[Virginia State College]], studying aerosol physics. In 1967, Darden earned an M.S. from Virginia State and taught classes there.<ref name="Oakes">{{cite book |last=Oakes |first=Elizabeth |date=2002 |title=International Encyclopedia of Women Scientists |location=New York |publisher=[[Facts on File]] |pages=[https://archive.org/details/internationalenc00oake/page/81 81–82] |isbn=0-8160-4381-7 |url=https://archive.org/details/internationalenc00oake/page/81 }}</ref>

=== Langley Research Center ===
In 1967, Darden started working as a [[human computer]] in the [[Langley Research Center]] computer pool at NASA. By that time, computers were increasingly used for the complex calculations to support engineering and design. The department, once tasked with processing scores of collected flight test data, by the 1940s had garnered a reputation as "human computers" who were essential to NASA's operation. During the 1950s and 1960s, more of these women gained opportunities to advance as technicians and engineers.<ref name="Atkinson">{{Cite web |last=Atkinson |first=Joe |date=2015-08-24 |title=From Computers to Leaders: Women at NASA Langley |url=http://www.nasa.gov/larc/from-computers-to-leaders-women-at-nasa-langley |access-date=2016-09-09 |publisher=NASA Langley}}</ref>

In 1983, Darden earned a D.Sc. in engineering from [[George Washington University]] and was promoted to [[Aerospace engineering|aerospace engineer]]. She specialized in analyzing supersonic noise.<ref name="nasa3">{{cite web |last1=Bradshaw |first1=Julia |title=Christine M. Darden |url=https://www.nasa.gov/langley/hall-of-honor/2022/christine-m-darden/ |website=NASA |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230313170638/https://www.nasa.gov/langley/hall-of-honor/2022/christine-m-darden/ |archive-date=13 March 2023 |date=11 July 2022 |url-status=live}}</ref> In 1989, Darden was appointed as leader of the sonic boom team, a subsidiary of the High Speed Research (HSR) Program. She worked on designs to decrease the negative effects of sonic booms, such as [[noise pollution]] and the [[depletion of the ozone layer]]. Her team tested new wing and nose designs for supersonic aircraft.<ref name="Oakes" />

The program was canceled by the government in February 1998, "without fan fare or press announcement."<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Reynolds|first=Randolph S.|date=2004|title=An Overview of the Demise of NASA's High Speed Research Program|url=http://commons.erau.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1536&context=jaaer |journal=Journal of Aviation/Aerospace Education & Research|volume=14|issue=1|doi=10.58940/2329-258X.1536 |s2cid=109477225 |access-date=September 8, 2016|doi-access=free}}</ref> 1998 abstract published by Darden describes the program as focused on "technologies needed for the development of an environmentally friendly, economically viable High-Speed Civil Transport [HSCT]."<ref name=dard3>{{Cite journal|last=Darden|first=Christine |date=September 11, 1998|title=An Overview of NASA's HSR Program: Environmental Issues and Economic Concerns|url=http://www.cs.odu.edu/~mln/ltrs-pdfs/NASA-98-eccmas-cmd.pdf |journal=European Community on Computational Methods in Applied Sciences}}</ref> Darden wrote more than 50 articles in the general field of aeronautical design, specializing in [[supersonic flow]] and flap design, as well as the prediction and minimization of sonic booms.

In 1999, Darden became the director of the Aero-Performing Center Management Office. She was the first African-American woman at Langley to be promoted into the [[Senior Executive Service (United States)|Senior Executive Service]], the top rank in the federal civil service.

In March 2007, Darden retired from NASA as director of the Office of Strategic Communication and Education.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.nasa.gov/centers/langley/news/researchernews/rn_07retirees.html|title=More Than 40 Take the Buyout, Retire|date=April 4, 2007|work=The Researcher News|access-date=September 8, 2016|archive-date=December 7, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221207052349/http://www.nasa.gov/centers/langley/news/researchernews/rn_07retirees.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

===Awards===
In 1985, Darden received the Dr. A. T. Weathers Technical Achievement Award from the [[National Technical Association]]. She received a [[Candace Award]] from the [[National Coalition of 100 Black Women]] in 1987.<ref name="page2">{{cite web |website=National Coalition of 100 Black Women |title=CANDACE AWARD RECIPIENTS 1982-1990, Page 2 |url=http://www.ncbw.org/programs/award2.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030314212510/http://www.ncbw.org/programs/award2.html |archive-date=March 14, 2003 }}</ref> She received three Certificates of Outstanding Performance from Langley Research Center: in 1989, 1991, and 1992.<ref name=Oakes/>

On January 28, 2018, Darden received the Presidential Citizenship Award at [[Hampton University]] in recognition for her contribution and service".<ref>{{Cite journal|date=January 24, 2018|title=Hampton University to celebrate Founder's Day with founder's great-grandson, alumni|url=http://www.dailypress.com/news/education/dp-nws-hampton-university-founders-day-2018-story.html|journal=Daily Press}}</ref>

Darden received an honorary degree from [[North Carolina State University]] on December 19, 2018.<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://news.ncsu.edu/2018/11/2018-fall-commencement-speech/ |title = NASA Engineer, Leader to Give NC State Fall Commencement Speech}}</ref>

Darden also received an honorary degree from the George Washington University on May 19, 2019.<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://gwtoday.gwu.edu/commencement-week-2019-what-you-need-know |title = Commencement Week 2019: What You Need to Know}}</ref>

In 2019, Darden was awarded the [[Congressional Gold Medal]].<ref name="congress" />

She delivered the Christine Darden Lecture at [[MathFest]] 2021.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Invited Addresses {{!}} Mathematical Association of America|url=https://www.maa.org/node/2567109/|access-date=2021-06-04|website=www.maa.org}}</ref>
